Series::center¶

Back to SeriesStatAccessor API Reference

Signature¶

Series::center() const -> Series
Series::center(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::stat.center(...) -> Series
Series::stat().center(...) -> Series

What It Does¶

center() subtracts a mean and preserves the original shape.

That one sentence is the heart of the method:

  • it removes location

  • it does not remove scale

  • it does not collapse dimensions

That makes it a transformation method rather than a summary statistic.

Compare the roles:

  • mean tells you the offset

  • center() removes the offset

So the real question answered by center() is:

What do these values look like once their average has been removed?

This is a good first normalization step whenever absolute level is less important than deviation around a local center.

Overload Map¶

center()

Subtract one global mean from the entire Series.

center(dim)

Subtract one mean per lane along the chosen axis, then broadcast that lane mean back over the original positions.

stat.center(...) / stat().center(...)

Equivalent accessor spellings. The accessor does not change the semantics; it just groups related statistical operations on a shared public surface.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t)

The axis whose lane means should be removed.

Important details:

  • dim = 0 means “work down the rows / along the first axis”

  • dim = 1 means “work across the columns / along the second axis”

  • negative dims count from the back, so -1 means the last axis

  • centering happens independently inside each lane selected by that axis

There is no keepdim flag because center() is not a reduction. The output already keeps the original shape.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as the input, but with the chosen mean removed.

Gradient¶

Centering is a linear transform, so it fits naturally inside ordinary differentiable numeric pipelines.

Examples¶

The examples below are intentionally progressive. They start with the global form, move to axis-aware centering, then show accessor spellings and edge behavior.

Unless stated otherwise, they use:

auto values = pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, {2, 3});

Example 1. Global centering removes one mean from the whole series.

std::cout << values.center();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-2.5, -1.5, -0.5],
  [0.5, 1.5, 2.5]]

The global mean is 3.5, so every element is shifted by that same amount.

Example 2. Row-wise centering removes one mean per row.

std::cout << values.stat.center(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-1, 0, 1],
  [-1, 0, 1]]

Each row is centered independently:

  • row 0 subtracts 2

  • row 1 subtracts 5

This is often the most useful form in practice because each row becomes locally mean-zero. The direct values.center(1) spelling follows the same semantics; this example uses the verified accessor call.

Example 3. The accessor spelling stat().center(dim) reaches the same operation.

std::cout << values.stat().center(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-1, 0, 1],
  [-1, 0, 1]]

This matters mostly for discoverability and style consistency. It is the same transformation as Example 2.

Example 4. Column-wise centering produces a different pattern because the lanes changed.

std::cout << values.center(0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-1.5, -1.5, -1.5],
  [1.5, 1.5, 1.5]]

Now each column is centered independently:

  • column 0 subtracts 2.5

  • column 1 subtracts 3.5

  • column 2 subtracts 4.5

Example 5. Negative dimensions count from the back, so -1 means the last axis.

std::cout << values.center(-1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-1, 0, 1],
  [-1, 0, 1]]

On this shape, the last axis is the row axis, so the result matches Example 2.

Example 6. A scalar Series centers to zero.

std::cout << pluss::make_series(42.0).center();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=0

That is a useful sanity check: if a Series has only one value, its mean is the value itself, so centering removes everything and leaves zero.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • center() always preserves shape. If you want a smaller result, you want a reduction such as mean, not center().

  • Global centering and axis-wise centering can produce very different outputs. Choosing the wrong dim is one of the easiest mistakes to make.

  • The centered values along the chosen lanes sum to zero up to ordinary floating arithmetic effects. That is one of the quickest ways to sanity-check the result.

  • A dim outside the valid axis range fails.

  • center() removes offset only. If you also want unit-scale output, use standardize.

Teaching Summary¶

Use center() when you want to preserve shape but remove average level:

  • center() removes one global mean

  • center(dim) removes one mean per lane

  • the accessor spellings are the same operation, just reached through stat

See Also¶

  • Series::standardize: centering plus scale normalization.

  • Series::mean: the reduction that computes the mean itself.
